title: Pick the right type
prompt: You need to store the sum of an array that can hold 10 million values, each up to 1,000,000. Which type?
options: `long` — the sum can reach 10^13, past int's ~2.1 x 10^9 limit
`int` — sums are always fine in int
`String` — numbers of any size fit in text
explanation: 10,000,000 x 1,000,000 = 10^13, far beyond Integer.MAX_VALUE (~2.1 x 10^9). Overflowing int silently wraps around to garbage values — a classic interview bug.

title: Print three values
prompt: Declare an `int` named `x` with value `42`, a `String` named `s` with value `"java"`, and a `boolean` named `ok` with value `true`. Print each on its own line using `System.out.println`.

solution.explanation: Each declaration names its type once; `println` prints any type followed by a newline, so three calls give three lines.

hints: Three values, three types: a whole number, some text, and a true/false.
Each declaration is `type name = value;` — for example `int x = 42;`

title: Complete the declarations
prompt: Fill in the missing types and suffix.
explanation: Whole number → `int`, decimal → `double`, single character → `char`. Literals bigger than int's max need the `L` suffix to be read as `long`.

title: What prints?
options: `7` — casting to int truncates toward zero
explanation: `(int)` chops off the decimal part. If you want rounding, use `Math.round(7.9)`.

title: Predict the output: division and casts
prompt: Predict exactly what each line prints.
explanation: `7 / 2` is int division → `3`. One `double` operand makes it real division → `3.5`. `double half = 7 / 2` still does int division first, then widens `3` to `3.0`. Casting to int truncates toward zero, so `-3.7` becomes `-3` (not `-4`).

title: Predict the output: overflow
prompt: Predict exactly what each line prints.
explanation: `Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1` wraps to `Integer.MIN_VALUE` = -2147483648 — no error, just a wrong number. `(long) a` makes the multiplication happen in `long`, so 100000 x 100000 = 10,000,000,000 fits.

title: Where does the cast go?
prompt: `int a = 100000, b = 100000;` Which line stores the correct product 10,000,000,000?
options: All three — the variable is a long
explanation: Casts bind tighter than `*`, so `(long) a * b` widens `a` first and the multiplication runs in `long`. In the other two, `a * b` is computed in `int`, overflows to 1410065408, and only then is widened — the damage is already done.

title: Recall: sentinel starting values
prompt: Fill in the constants that make any real value win the first comparison.
explanation: A running minimum starts at the largest possible value, a running maximum at the smallest. `Integer.MAX_VALUE` = 2147483647, `Integer.MIN_VALUE` = -2147483648; `Long` has the same pair.

title: Drill: declarations from memory
prompt: From a blank editor, write a full program (class `Main` with a `main` method) that declares an `int` `n = 7`, a `double` `d = 2.5`, a `String` `s = "go"`, then prints them each on their own line.

solution.explanation: Scaffold, three `type name = value;` declarations, three `println` calls — the order of prints decides the order of lines.

hints: You need the full program scaffold before any declarations.
Start with `public class Main { public static void main(String[] args) { ... } }`

title: Drill: overflow-safe product
prompt: From memory: return the exact product of `a` and `b` as a `long`. Inputs can be anywhere in the int range, so `a * b` in int would overflow.

solution.explanation: Casting one operand to `long` before `*` makes Java promote the other and multiply in 64 bits. `(long) (a * b)` would overflow first, then cast. O(1).

hints: Returning a `long` isn't enough — the multiplication itself has to happen in `long`.
Cast one operand before the `*`, not the result after it.
